I ran one job on IQM's free Garnet test device (garnet:mock). The job ID is 01a160a8-061e-7302-ab56-9029bb92506b. It held 6 circuits with 1000 shots each, and it completed. It cost 0 credits because it ran on the mock. The API still reports 1.0 billed second.

What I built: Each circuit holds 6 qubits, one per copper spin. Each circuit starts in the pattern up, down, up, down, up, down. It then evolves under the Heisenberg model H = J(SxSx + SySy + SzSz) with J = 1. I split the time into steps of 0.2 or less, which is called Trotter steps. Each step applies the pair interaction to every neighbor pair. The circuits stop at times 0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2, 1.6 and 2.0. The compiled circuits use 0, 28, 58, 88, 118 and 148 CZ gates. I read these numbers back from the job the server received.

What a perfect quantum computer would show: I simulated the submitted circuits without noise. The Neel order was 1.00, 0.88, 0.62, 0.41, 0.35 and 0.38 at those six times. The exact answer of the model is 1.00, 0.88, 0.62, 0.41, 0.34 and 0.37. The circuits match the physics to within about 0.01. The order starts perfect and drops by about two thirds by time 1.6. It then rises a little, because a short chain of 6 spins sloshes back and forth.

What the test device gave back: the Neel order values were -0.18, -0.40, -0.44, -0.41, -0.41 and -0.43. These numbers do not follow the circuit. The mock always returns a few fixed patterns such as 000000 and 111111 in about equal shares. It returned them even at time 0, where the answer must be exactly 1. The mock only checks that the job is valid and runs. It does not simulate the physics. A real run on Garnet would be needed to see the decay on hardware. With up to 148 CZ gates, hardware noise would likely pull the later values toward 0.

The principle: The perfect up-down pattern is not a stable state of the quantum Heisenberg model. The Sx Sx + Sy Sy part of the interaction lets a neighboring up and down spin swap places. These swaps spread through the chain and entangle the spins. That melts the alternating order within about one or two units of time.

What this says about KCuF3: The real chains in KCuF3 behave the same way. Quantum swaps between neighboring spins keep each chain from holding a perfect up-down order. Neutron scattering on KCuF3 sees a broad continuum of spin excitations, called spinons, instead of the sharp spin waves of an ordered magnet. KCuF3 does order below about 39 K. That order comes from weak coupling between the chains, and the ordered moment is much smaller than the full spin. Six spins is a small model and only shows a short time window. It still shows the same basic effect.
